blocks.text: Sandra Flores
Chief Operating Officer
{{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}}
Re: Capital Allocation Review for {{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}}
Dear Ms. Flores:

This letter sets down the terms on which our firm will assist {{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}} in examining how the company puts its capital to work across its businesses and where that capital might earn more than it does today, and it becomes our agreement at the moment you countersign the enclosed copy and return it to me. I have written it at some length and in plain terms, in the belief that an engagement of this kind proceeds far more surely when both parties have read the same account of it before any work begins, and I would ask you to measure what follows against your own recollection of our conversations and to tell me, before you sign, of any point on which your understanding and mine have not yet met.
The Review You Have Asked Us to Undertake

The work is a review of capital allocation, and its object is to help the company decide where its next increments of investment ought to go rather than to sit in judgment on decisions already taken. We will begin by establishing where the company's capital rests today, business by business and, where the records permit, project by project, together with what each part of the company has returned on the capital committed to it. From there we will consider the process by which reinvestment is decided and the hurdle to which a new commitment is held, marking the places where capital has settled into uses that no longer earn what it could earn elsewhere. We will then frame the choices that follow from that picture, whether they lie in concentrating capital where it compounds, releasing it from where it does not, or holding it against opportunities not yet in view, and we will weigh each choice against what it would require and what it could reasonably be expected to return.
How We Will Proceed

We will build from your own numbers rather than from a template, and we will document as we go, so that any figure reaching a deliverable can be traced back to a source your finance staff already recognize. We will keep our findings apart from our recommendations and label each for what it is, on the understanding that the two carry different weight and ought never to be mistaken for one another, and we will bring interim results to you as they firm up so that nothing in the final material arrives as a surprise. The review concludes with a recommendation and a plan your own people can carry out after we have gone.
The People Assigned to It

The engagement will be led day to day by Deborah Jimenez, an engagement manager of the firm, who will hold the work to its schedule, chair the working sessions, and serve as your first point of contact on any matter of substance. Brenda Clayton, a consultant, will carry the analysis beneath the review, from the reconciliation of the capital and return figures to the exhibits on which the findings will rest, and it is she your finance staff will hear from most often as the data is gathered. I read every deliverable before it leaves this office, and unless you direct us otherwise we will treat you, Sandra Flores, as our point of contact for scheduling and for the requests we make of your people.
Our Fee and When We Begin

Our fee to {{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}} for the review described above is a fixed {{fact:f:E-2019-003.fee}}, which covers that scope together with the ordinary meetings, correspondence, and interim materials the work entails. We will begin on {{fact:f:E-2019-003.start}}, and we have scoped the review to run approximately six months from that date to the final recommendation, though I will tell you early should the work prove to need more time or less.
Invoicing

We will invoice the fixed fee in equal monthly installments across the term, each installment falling due within thirty days of the date of its invoice. Out-of-pocket expenses, chiefly travel to your sites, are billed at cost, itemized on the invoice, and never marked up.
The Term and Its Ending

The engagement runs from the start date named above until we deliver the final recommendation, unless either of us brings it to an end sooner, which either party may do on fifteen days' written notice, for a reason or for none. Should it be ended early, {{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}} will owe the fee for the work performed to the effective date, prorated against the fixed fee, together with any expenses properly incurred, and we will hand over the work product in whatever state it has by then reached and assist an orderly close.
Confidentiality

We will treat the information you place in our hands as confidential, use it only for this review, and disclose it beyond our firm only as you direct in writing or as the law compels. A review of capital allocation necessarily reaches figures and intentions the company holds closely, and we will handle them with that squarely in mind; we ask the same of you as to our methods, our workpapers, and the terms of this fee, and these obligations will outlast the engagement itself.
The Limit of Our Liability

We will perform this work with the care and skill our profession expects, and our advice will represent our considered judgment on the information available to us; we do not, however, warrant any particular financial outcome, since so much of what follows a capital decision rests with your organization rather than with ours. Our total liability arising out of this engagement, on any theory, is limited to the fees actually paid to us under it, and neither party will be liable to the other for indirect or consequential loss, save that this limit does not reach a party's own fraud or willful misconduct.
Governing Law

This letter, together with the copy you countersign, is the whole of our agreement on this engagement and supersedes anything said or written before it, and it may be varied only in a writing signed by us both. It is governed by the law of the state in which our principal office sits, without regard to its conflict-of-laws rules, and any dispute we cannot settle between us will go to mediation before either party commences litigation.

If the terms above reflect our understanding, I would ask you to sign and date the enclosed copy and return it to me, keeping the second for your own file; on its arrival we will confirm the commencement and be ready to begin on the date set out above. If any part of it would be better talked through first, telephone me this week and I will make the time before you sign.
Sincerely,
To: Engagement Team
From: Brenda Clayton, Consultant
Re: Kickoff, Capital Allocation Review for {{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}}

We start on {{fact:f:E-2019-003.start}}. This memo sets the objective and the shape of the work so we begin from one reading of it. Our charge from {{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}} is narrow: help the company decide where its capital should go next, and what moving it would take. Everything we do serves that and nothing else. Where a question is interesting but off that line, we note it and set it aside.

Our contact on the client side is Sandra Flores, their Chief Operating Officer. Requests to their staff go through her office, so no one there is asked for the same file twice. Deborah Jimenez runs the engagement and sets the cadence; I hold the analysis and the exhibits beneath it. If you are unsure who owns a piece, ask early rather than guess.

The work runs about six months. I read it as three stretches: building the current picture and the returns, framing and testing the options, then the recommendation and the handover. We are at the very front of the first. That is where the time goes now, because every option we frame later is only as sound as the deployment and returns work under it.
How the work divides

items: Current deployment. Build the picture of where the company's capital sits today, business by business and, where the records allow, project by project. This is the base everything else stands on, so it goes first and I will not hurry it.

Returns on capital. For each business, tie the capital committed to what it has returned. Source every figure to the client's own ledger; we will be asked to show our working. Where shared overhead has to be split, agree the split before we cut the numbers, not after.

The allocation process. Document how reinvestment gets decided today and the hurdle a new commitment is held to. Note where the practice and the stated policy diverge, because that gap is usually where the recommendation lives.

Options and plan. Once the first three are solid, frame the reallocation options with what each requires and returns, then sequence the ones worth doing. This rests on the three above and must not run ahead of them.

blocks.text: How we keep the work

Two habits carry through all four workstreams. Every figure ties to a source in the client's own records, so a number can be traced back long after we have gone. And we label a finding as a finding and a recommendation as a recommendation, and never let the one drift into the other. When a number is soft, we mark it soft rather than round it into something firmer than it is.
This week

I will send the consolidated data request to Sandra Flores and get the kickoff session onto calendars. Deborah Jimenez, hold thirty minutes with me before that session so we agree what we are asking for and why; a tight first request saves us three follow-ups later. Keep a running log of every request and what comes back, so the first time a number is questioned we can show where it came from.

One assumption I do not want us carrying unexamined: that the way the company reports capital by business lines up with how the businesses actually run. If it does not, the returns work changes shape and some cuts will not tie. Flag it the moment the segment definitions arrive, while we can still act on it. The first task is mine, and the data request goes out the day we begin.
Hi Sandra,

We are underway and on plan. We have the first data pull and the capital-by-business history for {{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}}, and I have begun laying out where the company's capital sits today. The registers reconcile cleanly so far, which is a good sign this early. Deborah Jimenez has set the working-session cadence, so the analysis and your team's reviews move together rather than one waiting on the other.

One item is outstanding on your side. We still need the project-level returns for the two largest businesses. We can work from the business totals for now, but the project cut is what tells us whether the returns are broad or sitting in a handful of investments, and that difference changes the read. If your finance team can send it by the end of next week, we stay on schedule. If it will take longer, tell me and we will resequence around it.

Nothing else is needed from you today. For the first working session, our side will be Deborah Jimenez and Brenda Clayton; on yours, we would want you, Sandra Flores, and whoever owns the capital plan. I will send proposed times tomorrow so your assistants can hold the slots. An hour should cover this first one.
Sincerely
Working Session: Capital Deployment and Returns to Date

Recorded by Deborah Jimenez. These minutes cover the working session on the capital allocation review for {{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}} and follow the order of the discussion. Figures called provisional in the room are marked so here.
Attendees
Current Deployment

Brenda Clayton presented the map of where the company's capital sits today. The two largest businesses hold the majority of committed capital, with the balance spread thin across the rest. She marked this as a reading taken from the capital and asset registers, not a judgment on it. The registers reconcile to the general ledger for all but the third business, where the figures still come through at the segment total for part of the period. She is reconciling that period before she will call the figure firm. Sandra Flores confirmed the concentration in the largest business and named one investment not yet tied to the register, which was recorded for follow-up.
Returns on Capital

Brenda Clayton took the returns work as far as it has reached. Returns vary widely across the businesses: two earn well above the company's stated hurdle and one sits below it. Two limits were noted. The allocation of shared overhead is not yet settled, so the business-level returns should be read as provisional. The returns for the smallest business rest on a single year and need a longer base before they will hold. Deborah Jimenez asked that a range, not a single point, carry into the option work until the overhead allocation is fixed, and that was agreed. The team will not present a business-level return as firm while the overhead split is open.
The Allocation Process

Discussion turned to how reinvestment is decided today. There is a stated hurdle rate, but recent commitments do not consistently reflect it. Sandra Flores said the hurdle is applied unevenly across the businesses and asked that the review say so plainly. She noted that some commitments clear on strategic grounds that the hurdle never sees. Brenda Clayton will document both the stated policy and the practice, and mark where they part. No options were framed. It was agreed that options would be brought to the next session with their requirements and returns, and ranked only afterward.
Action Items

rows: Reconcile the open period in the third business and confirm the deployment figures
Settle the shared-overhead allocation and carry a range into the returns
Provide the additional investment tied to the largest business
Confirm interview times with the two business heads not yet met

blocks.text: The next step is the reconciliation of the open period. Until Brenda Clayton has closed it, the deployment figures stay provisional and the option work waits on them.
Capital Allocation Review for {{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}}

items: Progress report for the client's executive team
Status as of the midpoint of the review

blocks.text: Where things stand

The review is at its midpoint and on schedule. The current-deployment map and the returns-on-capital work are largely built, and the picture of where the company earns on its capital is now firm enough to reason from. The reallocation options are not yet framed, and none should be read into this report. We remain within the fixed budget of {{fact:f:E-2019-003.fee}}, with no change to scope and no expenses beyond the ordinary travel to your sites.

What has changed since the last update is that the analysis has moved from gathering to measurement. The registers are reconciled, the returns are cut, and the questions in front of us are now about what the numbers mean rather than whether we have them. That is the point in an engagement of this kind where the useful arguments start.
Done this period

We mapped where the company's capital sits today, business by business, and reconciled it to the asset and capital registers so the totals tie to numbers your finance staff already recognize. The reconciliation held for every business but one, where two months came through at the segment total; that gap is now closed. We tied committed capital to returns for every business but the smallest, which rests on too short a base to call firm and needs a longer history before we will present it.

We also documented how reinvestment is decided today and where the stated hurdle rate is applied unevenly across the businesses. Some commitments clear on strategic grounds the hurdle never tests, and we have set the stated policy and the actual practice side by side so the difference is visible. Deborah Jimenez held two working sessions with your team over the period, and the current-state read now matches what your operators recognize as their own.

Two findings are worth setting down plainly, though both remain provisional until the returns close. The committed capital is concentrated: the two largest businesses hold most of it, and the rest is spread thin. And the returns on that capital diverge sharply, with two businesses earning well above the hurdle and one below it. We present these as measurements, not yet as conclusions about what to do, and we will not turn a measurement into a recommendation before the evidence has earned it.
Coming up

Next we close the returns work on the smallest business and settle the shared-overhead allocation, which is the last thing holding the business-level returns as provisional. From there we frame the reallocation options, each with what it would require and what it could return, for discussion and not for decision. We expect to bring the closed current-state read and a first option set to the next working session, and to rank the options only after that discussion, not before it.
Budget and expenses

The engagement is a fixed-fee arrangement, and nothing in the work to date changes that. We are billing the fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2019-003.fee}} in equal monthly installments, as the engagement letter set out, and at the midpoint we are on that schedule with no overrun. Expenses have been limited to travel to your sites, billed at cost. We do not foresee anything that would carry the work beyond the fixed fee, and were that ever to change, we would tell you as soon as we saw it coming.
What could move the schedule

Two risks are worth naming now, while there is time to act on them. First, the overhead allocation is contested inside the company, and until it is settled the returns carry a range rather than a point. Second, the project-level detail for one business is still outstanding; without it, the option work there will rest on business totals and read coarser than the rest. Neither threatens the budget, but either could move the option framing by a week if it slips.
The one thing we need from your side is the outstanding project-level detail. With it in hand, the option framing holds its current date.
Working Session: Reallocation Options and the Draft Recommendation

Recorded by Deborah Jimenez. These minutes cover the working session on the capital allocation review for {{fact:f:E-2019-003.client}}. The session reviewed the ranked options and the shape of the recommendation. Points left open are marked as such.
Attendees
The Ranked Options

Brenda Clayton presented the reallocation options, now ranked. Three stand: concentrate capital in the two businesses earning above the hurdle, release capital from the business earning below it, and hold a reserve against the pipeline the operators described. The ranking rests on the returns work, which is now closed. The shared-overhead allocation that had held the returns provisional has been settled, and the business-level returns are firm. Each option carries what it would require and what it could return, so the ranking can be taken apart rather than taken on trust. Sandra Flores agreed with the top of the ranking and questioned the size of the reserve, which was noted for the recommendation.
The Business Below the Hurdle

Most of the discussion was on the business earning below the hurdle. Brenda Clayton was careful to separate the finding from the recommendation: the returns are measured and firm, but whether to release the capital or to fix the business is a decision for the company. She walked through what a fix would demand and what it might recover, without recommending it. Sandra Flores said the board would want both paths costed before it chose, and that a single course would not survive the board's questions. It was agreed the recommendation would present the release option alongside a brief fix-or-hold alternative, rather than a single course.
Toward the Recommendation and Handover

The remaining work is the recommendation and the materials the company keeps. Brenda Clayton will assemble the final read and the exhibits so the company's own staff can rerun the returns after the engagement closes. The workpapers will be handed over labeled and sourced, not as a black box. Deborah Jimenez will arrange the closing session with the executive team and confirm who from the board should attend. No new analysis is open; what remains is drafting, review, and handover.
Action Items

rows: Cost the fix-or-hold alternative for the business below the hurdle
Size the reserve option against the operators' pipeline
Confirm the board's questions to be answered in the recommendation
Arrange the closing session with the executive team

blocks.text: The next step is the fix-or-hold costing. The recommendation cannot be finalized until Brenda Clayton has it and the reserve is sized.
